ai.literal: Those who dig (it) / bears / earth / like / oneself / those who insult / bearing / foremost.
ai.translation: Just as the earth bears those who dig into it, bearing with those who insult oneself is the foremost virtue.
ai.modern: தன்னைத் தோண்டுபவர்களையும் தாங்குகின்ற பூமியைப் போல, தன்னை அவமதிப்பவர்களையும் பொறுத்துக்கொள்வதே மிகச் சிறந்த பண்பாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a powerful natural simile to define the highest form of forbearance. The earth does not punish those who dig into it; instead, it continues to support them. In the same way, the greatest virtue is to patiently endure and forgive those who insult or harm us. The word 'தலை' literally means 'head', but is used metaphorically here to mean the foremost or highest quality.

ai.literal: Bearing transgression always, that forgetting even than that is good.
ai.translation: It is always good to endure a transgression, but forgetting it is even better.
ai.modern: பிறர் செய்யும் குற்றத்தை எப்போதும் பொறுத்துக்கொள்வது நல்லது. ஆனால் அக்குற்றத்தை மனதிலிருந்து முற்றிலும் மறந்துவிடுவது பொறுத்துக்கொள்வதையும் விட மிகவும் சிறந்தது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two noble responses to someone else's wrongdoing. The word 'iṟappu' can mean death or passing, but here it takes the sense of a transgression or an act that goes beyond acceptable limits. While 'poṟuttal' (bearing or forgiving) such an act is always a virtuous practice, 'maṟattal' (completely forgetting the offense) is praised as even better. This is because merely forgiving might still leave a trace of the wrong in the mind, whereas forgetting removes the memory entirely, ensuring absolute inner peace.

ai.literal: Among poverty, poverty is guest rejecting; among strength, strength is fools bearing.
ai.translation: The worst poverty is turning away guests; the greatest strength is bearing with the ignorant.
ai.modern: வறுமையிலும் கொடிய வறுமை வந்த விருந்தினரை ஏற்காமல் தவிர்ப்பது ஆகும்; வலிமையிலும் சிறந்த வலிமை அறிவற்றவர்கள் செய்யும் பிழைகளைப் பொறுத்துக்கொள்வது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet uses a parallel structure to contrast the worst kind of lack with the best kind of power. The phrase poverty within poverty refers to the extreme destitution of being unable or unwilling to host guests. Conversely, strength within strength defines true power not as physical force, but as the forbearance to tolerate the offenses of the ignorant. By placing these concepts side by side, the poet emphasizes that moral endurance is the ultimate strength.

ai.literal: Possession of perfection not leaving if desired, possession of forbearance having cherished to conduct oneself is required.
ai.translation: If you desire your perfection of character to never leave you, you must cherish and practice forbearance.
ai.modern: நிறைக்குணம் தம்மை விட்டு நீங்காமல் இருக்க வேண்டும் என்று ஒருவர் விரும்பினால், அவர் பொறுமையைப் போற்றிக் கடைப்பிடிக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet teaches that true perfection of character cannot endure without patience. If one desires their inner completeness and goodness to never leave them, they must actively cherish and practice forbearance. The word 'niṟaiyuṭaimai' signifies the possession of a full, unblemished moral character. By using the word 'pōṟṟi', the poet emphasizes that patience is a precious treasure that must be carefully guarded and maintained in all actions.

ai.literal: Those who retaliated, as a thing of value they will not esteem indeed; they will esteem those who endured, like gold having treasured.
ai.translation: The wise will not consider those who retaliate as having any worth. But they will treasure those who endure wrongs, keeping them safe like gold.
ai.modern: தீங்கு செய்தவரைத் தண்டிப்பவர்களைச் சான்றோர் ஒரு பொருட்டாக மதிக்க மாட்டார்கள். ஆனால், பொறுத்துக்கொள்பவர்களைப் பொன்னைப்போலப் போற்றித் தம் மனத்துள் வைத்துக்கொள்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the vengeful with the forgiving. The word 'ஒன்றாக' literally means 'as one', but here takes the sense of 'as a thing of value' or 'as something that matters'. The wise do not give any regard to those who retaliate against wrongs. However, they highly esteem those who practice forbearance, holding them in their minds just as one would carefully wrap and protect precious gold.

ai.literal: To those who punished, one day's pleasure; to those who forbore, until-perishing glory.
ai.translation: Those who punish an offense find pleasure for a single day, but those who bear it patiently gain glory that lasts until the end of time.
ai.modern: பிறர் செய்த தவற்றைத் தண்டிப்பவருக்கு அந்த ஒரு நாள் மட்டுமே இன்பம் கிடைக்கும். ஆனால் அதனைப் பொறுத்துக்கொள்பவருக்கு உலகம் அழியும் வரை புகழ் நிலைத்திருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the fleeting satisfaction of retaliation with the enduring legacy of forgiveness. The phrase 'oru nāḷai iṉpam' highlights that punishing an offender offers only a brief, single day of emotional release. In contrast, 'poṉṟum tuṇaiyum pukaḻ' reveals that choosing to patiently bear an offense earns a person glory that lasts until the very end of time. By juxtaposing these two outcomes, the poet emphasizes that true greatness lies in forbearance rather than revenge.

ai.literal: Proper things not-they to oneself others even if do, pain having grieved, virtue not-they non-doing is good.
ai.translation: Even if others do improper things to you, it is good to grieve for the pain it causes and refrain from doing unvirtuous things in return.
ai.modern: பிறர் தனக்குத் தகுதியற்ற தீமைகளைச் செய்தாலும், அதனால் வரும் துன்பத்திற்காக வருந்தி, அறமல்லாத செயல்களைத் தான் செய்யாதிருத்தல் நல்லது.
ai.explanation: The couplet teaches that one should not retaliate against those who do wrong. The word 'திறனல்ல' refers to actions that are improper or unjust. When others commit such acts against us, we should feel sorrow ('நோ நொந்து') for the pain that evil inevitably brings, rather than seeking revenge. True forbearance is choosing not to commit unvirtuous acts ('அறனல்ல செய்யாமை'), thereby breaking the cycle of harm.

ai.explanation: This couplet teaches the ultimate response to arrogant provocation. When others commit excesses or wrongs out of pride, one should not retaliate in kind. Instead, one should defeat them through one's own noble character and forbearance, effectively neutralizing their malice with dignified patience.

ai.literal: Than those who have renounced, purity they possess, transgressors' mouth harsh words those who can endure.
ai.translation: Those who can endure harsh words from the mouths of transgressors possess a purity greater than that of ascetics.
ai.modern: வரம்பு மீறியவர்களின் வாயிலிருந்து வரும் கடுமையான சொற்களைப் பொறுத்துக்கொள்பவர்கள், பற்றுகளைத் துறந்த முனிவர்களை விடவும் தூய்மையானவர்கள் ஆவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet compares the virtue of patience with the purity of renunciation. It states that those who can patiently endure harsh words from people who transgress boundaries of decency are purer than ascetics who have renounced the world. The word 'இறந்தார்' refers to those who have crossed the limits of proper conduct, while 'நோற்கிற்பவர்' highlights the active strength required to bear their insults. Thus, true purity lies not just in leaving the world, but in maintaining one's composure amidst its provocations.

ai.literal: Without eating those who do penance are great, (but they are) behind than those who endure harsh words that others say.
ai.translation: Those who do penance by fasting are great, but they rank behind those who patiently endure the harsh words of others.
ai.modern: உணவு உண்ணாமல் விரதம் இருப்பவர்கள் பெரியவர்கள் தான்; ஆனால் அவர்கள், மற்றவர்கள் சொல்லும் கடுமையான சொற்களைப் பொறுத்துக்கொள்பவர்களுக்கு அடுத்த நிலையில் தான் இருப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two types of endurance: physical fasting and emotional forbearance. The root word 'நோல்' is used twice, first meaning 'to do penance' by fasting, and second meaning 'to endure' harsh words. The poet declares that while fasting is a mark of greatness, the mental strength required to patiently bear the insults of others is an even higher virtue. Therefore, ascetics who fast rank only 'behind' (பின்) those who practice true forbearance.
